clinicalPearls: An abnormally high haematocrit in the newborn, conventionally a venous value above the mid-sixties percent
The clinical concern is hyperviscosity, which impairs microcirculatory flow
Causes include placental transfusion (delayed cord clamping, twin-to-twin transfusion), intrauterine hypoxia and maternal diabetes
Many infants are asymptomatic; symptoms are non-specific and include plethora, lethargy, poor feeding, jitteriness and hypoglycaemia
Capillary samples overestimate haematocrit, so a venous sample is needed to confirm
Partial exchange transfusion is considered for symptomatic infants with significant polycythaemia, alongside hydration and treating hypoglycaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Neonatal polycythaemia results from either increased red cell transfusion to the fetus or newborn (as with delayed cord clamping, cord stripping or twin-to-twin transfusion) or increased fetal red cell production in response to chronic intrauterine hypoxia (as in growth restriction, maternal diabetes or maternal smoking). As the haematocrit rises, blood viscosity increases disproportionately, impairing flow through the microcirculation and reducing oxygen and glucose delivery to tissues. This underlies complications affecting the brain, gut, kidneys and metabolic status, and increases the risk of hypoglycaemia and jaundice.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis (as a cause of similar non-specific symptoms)
additionalInvestigations: Evaluation for underlying cause and for complications where symptomatic
redFlags: Neurological signs such as seizures or marked lethargy
Features of necrotising enterocolitis or renal compromise
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic infants generally do well with hydration and monitoring; symptomatic hyperviscosity, particularly with end-organ effects, carries a less certain neurodevelopmental prognosis.
pitfalls: Acting on a capillary rather than venous haematocrit
Overlooking hypoglycaemia in a polycythaemic infant
Attributing symptoms to polycythaemia without excluding sepsis
management: Ensure adequate hydration and fluid intake for asymptomatic infants with a modestly raised haematocrit
Perform partial exchange transfusion, replacing blood with crystalloid, for symptomatic infants with significant hyperviscosity
Confirm polycythaemia on a venous haematocrit, as capillary samples overestimate the value
Treat accompanying hypoglycaemia and monitor bilirubin for hyperbilirubinaemia
Observe for end-organ effects on the brain, gut and kidneys, including necrotising enterocolitis once enteral feeding begins
Evaluate and address the underlying cause such as maternal diabetes, intrauterine hypoxia or placental transfusion
